canonical_concept.beeja: ॐ (Om/Auṃ) — the primordial sound that is the sonic form of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad opens: "Auṃ ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvam" — Om, this syllable is all this.
canonical_concept.vyakarana: Brahman is a neuter noun (not to be confused with Brahmā, the masculine creator deity, or Brāhmaṇa, the priestly class). Derived from the root bṛh with the suffix -man. The neuter gender indicates that Brahman transcends all categories including gender.
canonical_concept.functional_meaning: Brahman is the infinite, eternal, unchanging absolute reality that is the ground of all existence. It is both the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) and the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) of the universe. Brahman is described via two approaches: Nirguṇa Brahman (without attributes — the absolute beyond all description) and Saguṇa Brahman (with attributes — the personal God, Īśvara). The Upaniṣads teach that Brahman is identical with Ātman (the individual Self).
canonical_concept.dhatu: बृह् (Bṛh) — To expand, to grow, to be great.
canonical_concept.nirukta: Yāska: "bṛhati iti brahma" — that which is great, that which expands. Brahman is the infinitely expanding reality that underlies all existence.
canonical_concept.tattva: Brahma-Tattva — the principle of absolute, infinite, self-luminous reality. Brahman is described as Sat-Cit-Ānanda (Being-Consciousness-Bliss) — not three qualities but three aspects of one indivisible reality.

claims.value: In Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Brahman alone is real (Brahma satyam); the world is appearance (jagat mithyā); the individual self is Brahman (jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ). In Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Brahman is real, personal (Viṣṇu), and the universe and souls are Brahman's body. In Dvaita (Madhva): Brahman (Viṣṇu) is real and eternally distinct from souls and world. In Śaiva Siddhānta: Brahman is Śiva, the supreme reality with infinite śaktis.

claims.value: Brahman is the source, sustainer, and dissolution point of all universes. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante" — from which all beings are born, by which they live, into which they return — that is Brahman. The Purāṇas describe Brahman as the ocean from which the universe arises like waves. The concept of Brahmaṇḍa (Brahman's egg) is the cosmic egg from which the universe hatches.

claims.value: Brahman as psychological reality: the deepest layer of consciousness is Brahman. In Yoga psychology, the state of samādhi (absorption) is the direct experience of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad identifies Brahman with the fourth state of consciousness (turīya) that underlies waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. The experience of Brahman is described as "neti neti" (not this, not this) — Brahman cannot be grasped by the mind but is the ground of the mind.

claims.value: The concept of Brahman in governance: the ideal ruler is one who has realized Brahman and governs from that realization. The Arthaśāstra's concept of the philosopher-king parallels the Upaniṣadic ideal of the Brahman-realized ruler. The concept of Brahma-rāṣṭra (the kingdom of Brahman) appears in Vedic literature as the ideal polity.

claims.value: In Āyurveda: Brahman is the ultimate source of health (ārogya). The concept of Brahma-cakra (the cycle of Brahman) underlies the Āyurvedic understanding of the body as a microcosm of the universe. The highest healing is Brahma-jñāna (knowledge of Brahman) which removes the root cause of all disease — avidyā (ignorance).

claims.value: The concept of Brahman in mathematics: Brahman as the infinite (ananta) is the philosophical basis for the Indian mathematical concept of infinity. The concept of śūnya (zero) as the void from which all numbers emerge mirrors the Brahman-as-source concept. The Upaniṣadic statement "pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam" (that is full, this is full) is a mathematical statement about the nature of infinity.

The concept of Brahma-muhūrta (the hour of Brahman — 1.5 hours before sunrise) is the most auspicious time for spiritual practice. The Milky Way (Ākāśagaṅgā) is considered the visible form of Brahman's cosmic body.

claims.value: Om (ॐ) is the primary symbol of Brahman — the sound of the universe. The infinite space (ākāśa) symbolizes Brahman's all-pervading nature. The ocean symbolizes Brahman — waves (individual beings) arise from and return to the ocean. The sun symbolizes Nirguṇa Brahman — self-luminous, the source of all light. The bindu (point) in the center of a yantra represents Brahman as the source of all manifestation.

retrieved_evidence.content: The Upanishads expound the secret meaning of the Vedas and treat of Brahma, according to [2]. They are considered the crowning part of the Veda, providing knowledge about the ultimate reality and the self. [1] also mentions the importance of being properly instructed by knowers of the Brahman, implying that the Upanishads contain teachings on spiritual growth and self-realization.

The Taittiriya Upanishad explains Brahman as the Supreme Self, entirely distinct from the world, and as the source of everything [1]. It describes Brahman as the unconditioned, non-dual bliss, beyond the scope of speech and thought, and as indescribable and incomprehensible [2].

The meaning of "ब्रह्म (Brahman)" is the Supreme or Ultimate Reality, which is described in the Vedas as the absolute and imperishable essence of the universe [1]. It can refer to the visible universe inclusive of individual souls or to the Ultimate Reality behind it, experienced in Samadhi as the Self of ourselves [1]. According to the Advaitic explanation, Brahman is above the world of cause and effect [1].

pipeline.value: Brahman is the infinite, eternal, unchanging absolute reality that is the ground of all existence. It is both the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) and the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) of the universe. Brahman is described via two approaches: Nirguṇa Brahman (without attributes — the absolute beyond all description) and Saguṇa Brahman (with attributes — the personal God, Īśvara). The Upaniṣads teach that Brahman is identical with Ātman (the individual Self).
